title: It now seems possible to vaccinate against cancer

vocab.articleQuote: Billions have been spent, yet the field is notorious for its broken promises.
vocab.meaning: Notorious means famous, but only ever for something bad. A notorious intersection is one everybody knows is dangerous, and a notorious cheater is widely known for cheating, which is why you can never be notorious for kindness. Calling the cancer-vaccine field notorious tells you it is not some obscure corner of science nobody noticed. Everyone in medicine knows the field, and what they know it for is decades of announcements that led nowhere.
examples: That corner by the school gate is notorious for fender benders, so a crossing guard stands there every morning.
Our group chat is notorious for going completely silent the night before a project is due.

vocab.articleQuote: First the caveats: delaying re-occurrence might extend overall survival, but it also might not.
vocab.meaning: A caveat is a warning or a condition attached to a claim, the sentence beginning "but keep in mind" that stops you believing more than the evidence supports. It comes from the Latin for "let him beware." Here the writer reports that the vaccine slowed the return of melanoma and then immediately lists three caveats: a delay might not actually lengthen anyone's life, the benefit might be small next to an enormous price, and melanoma might be an unusually easy cancer to attack. Naming your own caveats is a sign of careful thinking rather than of weak evidence.
examples: I'll drive you to practice, with one caveat: if it rains, we leave twenty minutes earlier.
He said the recipe was easy, though the caveat was that the dough had to sit in the fridge overnight.

vocab.articleQuote: The interim results show the vaccine is indeed working, and by implication that the neoantigen idea works, too.
vocab.meaning: Interim means in between and temporary, filling a gap until the real or final version arrives. A school with an interim principal has someone holding the job until a permanent one is hired, and an interim report is a progress update rather than a conclusion. In a drug trial, interim results are what researchers can see partway through, before the study has run its full course. That one word is carrying a lot of weight in this article, because it separates "the vaccine is working so far" from "the vaccine works."
examples: Our teacher posts interim grades in October so we know where we stand well before finals.
Until the school hires a new coach in the spring, an interim coach is running our practices.

concepts.name: Antigens
concepts.articleQuote: The idea of a cancer vaccine is to alert the immune system to mutated proteins, known as neoantigens, found in tumours.
concepts.meaning:
The article says the idea is to alert the immune system. Nothing in your body is waiting for an alert, and taking that phrase literally is the fastest way to misunderstand everything that follows. An antigen is a molecule, or a short piece of one, that an immune cell can stick to. Immunology, the study of how bodies defend themselves, is to a large extent the study of which molecules stick to which.

That raises the obvious question. If this is all molecules attaching to each other, how does anything end up being treated as foreign? Not by any judgment. T cells finish developing inside the thymus, an organ behind the breastbone, and while they are there, any T cell whose receptor sticks strongly to the body's own molecules is destroyed before it ever reaches the bloodstream. Huge numbers are destroyed this way. What is left is a population of cells that do not stick to you. After that, foreign means one thing only: a shape that one of the surviving receptors happens to fit.

The cases where this goes wrong show that it really does work that way. Pollen cannot hurt anyone, and it causes hay fever. A transplanted kidney is saving the patient's life, and the body destroys it unless that patient takes drugs every day for the rest of their life. Neither one is dangerous. Both simply carry shapes that some surviving receptor fits.

One more piece of machinery matters here, because the rest of this story runs on it. Cells break down a fraction of the proteins they build into short pieces, and other molecules carry those pieces out to the cell surface and hold them there, facing outward. This happens constantly, in almost every cell you have. The outside of a cell therefore carries small samples of the proteins being built inside it, where the receptors of a passing T cell can reach them.

Now the article's word needs no extra explanation. Neo means new. A neoantigen is one of those exposed pieces that no cell in the body has ever carried before, because the gene it came from was damaged and now builds a slightly different protein. It is not foreign in the sense of having come from outside. It is new, which under the rule above amounts to the same thing.

The idea to carry: whenever you read that an immune system detects or recognises something, translate it into shapes fitting together, with no decision anywhere in the process. Allergies, transplant rejection and this vaccine all fall out of that one substitution.

concepts.name: T cells
concepts.articleQuote: If the system clocks these as foreign it will eliminate cells that have them.
concepts.meaning:
The article says the immune system will eliminate cells carrying mutated proteins. The cell that does the eliminating is a T cell, which the article never mentions, and that omission is what makes the sentence hard to picture. A T cell is a type of white blood cell. The T is for the thymus, where it finishes developing. You have hundreds of billions of them, and each one carries many thousands of copies of a single receptor shape on its outer surface.

T cells move through blood and tissue and come into brief physical contact with other cells. During that contact one of two things happens. If the receptors on the T cell bind to the protein pieces held on the outside of the other cell, that binding starts a chain of chemical changes inside the T cell, and it releases proteins that make pores in the other cell's membrane and start the process that makes that cell break itself down. Biologists call that process apoptosis. If the receptors do not bind, the contact ends and nothing further happens. Binding or not binding is the whole difference, and there is no assessment step in between.

A cell that kills other cells on contact is a dangerous thing to have circulating, and it does go wrong. When T cells destroy healthy tissue the result is an autoimmune disease: in type 1 diabetes, T cells destroy the insulin-producing cells of the pancreas. So there is a second binding step that stops the killing. Many healthy cells carry a particular molecule on their surface, and T cells carry a receptor that this molecule fits. When those two bind, the chemical chain inside the T cell is shut down and no killing follows. That pair of molecules is what the word checkpoint refers to.

The article's line about tumours suppressing an immune response can now be stated exactly. Cancer cells divide constantly with damaged DNA, so they vary from one another. A cancer cell that happens to make more of that stop molecule is not killed on contact and goes on dividing. One that makes less is killed, and its copies are gone with it. After some months most cells in the tumour make a lot of it. None of this is a strategy and the tumour has not worked anything out. The cells without the molecule were removed, so the ones you find are the ones that had it.

A checkpoint inhibitor is a molecule built to bind one half of that pair before the other half can. While it is attached, the tumour's stop molecule and the T cell's receptor cannot reach each other, the shutdown never starts, and the T cell kills the cell it is touching. The side effects follow directly from the same fact: with that stop step blocked everywhere in the body, T cells sometimes destroy healthy tissue, so patients on these drugs can develop autoimmune problems.

Worth carrying out the door: an off switch is usually not a flaw in a system, it is the reason the system is safe to have at all. When something takes advantage of an off switch, the fix is rarely to remove it. Here the fix is to block it temporarily and accept the damage that blocking it does.

concepts.name: Antibodies
concepts.articleQuote: using mRNA technology developed for vaccination against infections
concepts.meaning:
Ask most people how a vaccine works and the answer is antibodies. That answer is right about every vaccine they have had and wrong about this one, and the difference comes down to a physical limit that is worth knowing.

An antibody is a protein, roughly Y-shaped, built and released by a B cell, which is the other main kind of lymphocyte alongside the T cell. Unlike a T cell receptor, an antibody is not attached to any cell. Millions of copies of it move freely in blood and lymph. Each antibody has two ends shaped to bind one particular molecular shape, and when it meets that shape on the outer surface of a virus particle or a bacterium, it attaches and stays attached. Two useful things follow. The antibody physically occupies the part of the virus that would otherwise attach to one of your cells, so that virus can no longer get in. And other immune cells carry receptors for the stem of the antibody, so a particle coated in antibodies is engulfed and broken down. That is what most vaccines produce: your body builds antibodies against a shape found on a virus before you ever meet it, so the virus is bound and cleared while it is still in the blood.

Here is the limit that decides this article's whole approach. An antibody is a large protein and cannot cross a cell membrane, so it can only ever bind to something on the outside of a cell. A virus travelling in the bloodstream is reachable. The same virus, once inside one of your cells, is not. And a cancer cell is one of your own cells, with its mutated protein being built inside it.

So a vaccine aimed at your own cancer cannot work the way a flu shot works, because there is nothing floating in the blood to bind to. The only place that mutated protein becomes reachable at all is the piece of it the cell carries on its outer surface, and the cells whose receptors bind those pieces are T cells. That is why this melanoma vaccine is built to produce T cells rather than antibodies. The article never says so, because to an immunologist it goes without saying.

One fact ties the two halves together. Checkpoint inhibitors, the drugs given alongside this vaccine, are themselves antibodies. They are not made by the patient's B cells, they are manufactured, and the shape they bind is not part of a virus but the stop molecule on the surface of a cell. Antibodies used as medicines are now everywhere in hospitals, and nearly all of them work this way: a protein chosen because it binds one specific thing and blocks it.

The general point: your immune system has two parts that reach different places. Antibodies deal with what is outside cells, and T cells deal with what is inside them. So when someone says a treatment boosts the immune system, the useful question is which part, because help aimed at the wrong one cannot physically reach the problem.

quiz.question: The article says the cancer-vaccine field "is notorious for its broken promises." What is that telling you about the field?
options: It is a small, obscure corner of research that few scientists have bothered with
It is widely known, and what it is known for is repeatedly failing to deliver
Its published results have been shown to be deliberately faked
Regulators have refused to allow research in it
quiz.explanation: Notorious means famous specifically for something bad, so the field is well known in medicine and known for decades of announcements that came to nothing.

quiz.question: The article says the immune system acts if it "clocks these as foreign." What actually decides whether something counts as foreign?
options: Whether the substance is harmful to the body
Whether an immune cell carries a receptor whose shape binds it, since receptors that bind the body's own molecules are destroyed while those cells are developing
Whether the substance originally came from outside the body
Whether the substance is a protein rather than a fat or a sugar
quiz.explanation: Harmless pollen causes allergies and a life-saving transplanted kidney gets destroyed, so danger is not the test; what matters is whether a surviving receptor binds that shape.

quiz.question: Why is the melanoma vaccine given together with a checkpoint inhibitor rather than on its own?
options: The checkpoint inhibitor stops the vaccine breaking down in the bloodstream
Many cancer cells carry a molecule that binds a receptor on the T cell and shuts down its killing, and the inhibitor binds one half of that pair first so the two cannot reach each other
The checkpoint inhibitor destroys the tumour while the vaccine prevents infection after surgery
Drug regulators require every cancer trial to test two drugs together
quiz.explanation: A T cell stops killing when that pair of molecules binds, so a vaccine that produces T cells achieves nothing until the inhibitor blocks that step.

quiz.question: Why can a vaccine against your own cancer not work the way a flu shot works, by producing antibodies?
options: Antibodies are too small to bind to something as large as a cancer cell
An antibody cannot cross a cell membrane, so it only reaches the outside of cells, and a cancer cell's mutated protein is built inside it
The body stops producing new antibodies in adulthood
Antibodies bind only to bacteria, never to viruses or to human cells
quiz.explanation: Antibodies work on things outside cells, such as a virus in the blood, so reaching a protein made inside one of your own cells is a job for T cells instead.

quiz.question: The article reports interim results and then immediately lists its caveats. Which of these is NOT one of the caveats it raises?
options: Delaying the return of the cancer might not actually mean patients live longer
The benefit could turn out to be small while the treatment is enormously expensive
Melanoma provokes the immune system unusually strongly, so other cancers may respond less well
Personalised vaccines cannot be manufactured quickly enough for individual patients
quiz.explanation: A caveat is a warning attached to a claim, and the article raises the first three; manufacturing speed is the problem mRNA technology already solved, not a remaining doubt.
